title: How the One Becomes the Many
reflection: Once or twice this week, when the past or the future weighs on you, pause. Notice: I am building this memory right now, or I am generating this worry right now. Then notice the awareness they appear in.

questions.q: Kai says that “the world is an illusion” sounds like a cop-out. How does Swamiji explain māyā?
o: Not that the world is fake, but that it is not what it first appears: distinctions are real, not ultimate.
That the world is fake and pain unreal, so the right response is to rise above it and to cease to care.
That the world is a dream that a person wakes from once, after which nothing in it can matter again.
That the world is a trick played by others, so the right response is to be on guard against everyone.
questions.e: Swamiji says that translation has done real harm and the course flatly rejects it. Joy and pain are felt, actions have consequences and relationships matter. Māyā is the principle by which the one Reality appears as the many.

questions.q: White light passes through a prism and fans into colours. Which point does Swamiji draw from this?
o: The colours are real and distinct but not separate from the light: difference is not separation.
The colours are unreal, since only the white light is there, and the rainbow is only a trick of the eye.
The colours are separate substances, each arriving from somewhere else and joining the light briefly.
The colours spoil the light, so the best view of reality is the one before it is spread out.
questions.e: The colours are the light, articulated. Like the waves of the ocean in the previous lesson, one living awareness appears as knower and known, self and world, you and me, each real and none a separate substance floating free.

questions.q: James says the error is not seeing differences but thinking they go all the way down. Which example from the lesson shows a useful distinction hardening into a wall?
o: “I am a mother” hardening into “I am only a mother”: worth then rises and falls with her children.
“I am hungry” becoming “I am thirsty,” so Sarah has to look after her body in two quite different ways.
“This is food” and “this is poison,” so Sarah must tell the two apart before she can feed her children well.
“This is my child” and “that is another child,” so Sarah cannot love anyone outside of her own family.
questions.e: Telling food from poison or your child from another’s is useful; life depends on it. The trouble comes when a working label becomes absolute: I am only this body makes ageing and illness terror. Swamiji says bondage is not the difference itself but the forgetting of the unity within the difference.
questions.c: A useful label hardens into a wall

questions.q: Which three conditions does the lesson name as the scaffolding that turns a field of differences into the ordered world we live in?
o: Space, time and causation.
Mind, body and spirit.
Light, sound and touch.
Birth, growth and decay.
questions.e: Space lets things be here and there; time gives before and after, change, memory and anticipation; causation links events so that the world hangs together as a process. They are real and indispensable for living, yet not the final truth of me.
questions.c: Space, time and causation are the scaffolding

questions.q: “Einstein showed that space and time are fixed, absolute containers, and the contemplatives agree that they are the bedrock of what you are.”
questions.e: The reverse. Space can contract and time dilate, and two events simultaneous for one observer can be sequential for another, so there is no universal now. The contemplatives said from inside that space, time and causation belong to the expressed world, the flow, not to the deepest ground.
questions.c: Space and time are relational, not the bedrock

questions.q: Sarah assumes a painful memory is an exact recording. What does neuroscience find, according to Swamiji?
o: Each memory is rebuilt and coloured by present mood, and imagining the future uses almost the same machinery.
Memory is an exact recording, so a painful memory is simply a true fact that has to be endured for life.
Memory is rebuilt only in the first years of life, so an adult’s memories stay the same ever after that.
Memory and imagination use different parts of the brain, so a remembered past is never like an imagined future.
questions.e: When you picture next week you are not reading a fixed file, you are generating a simulation out of bits of the past. So the past and the future we live with are constructed right now, in present awareness.

questions.q: Kai describes low evenings of replaying old failures. How does Swamiji read depression and anxiety in this light?
o: Depression suffers a past rebuilt by low mood, anxiety a simulated future: both are present constructions.
Depression suffers the actual past and anxiety the actual future, so the suffering is fixed by what happened.
Depression and anxiety are failures to forget, so the cure is to push the past and future from the mind.
Depression and anxiety are only in the head, so the sufferer should just get over them and carry on.
questions.e: James asks that it not sound dismissive, and Swamiji agrees: the suffering is completely real because the construction is really happening. What changes is that you see what kind of thing it is, and that makes it workable.
questions.c: Haunting past and frightening future are built now

questions.q: What is the “spine of the course” that Swamiji says Kai has put his finger on?
o: Two faces of one Reality: the still, living ground and the flow of time-building dynamism, one Consciousness-Energy.
Two separate realities: a still ground that is real and a moving world that is unreal and best ignored by us.
Two stages of a life: a time of movement while young and a time of stillness when a person is older.
Two schools of thought: a Vedanta school that prefers the ground and a Trika school that prefers the flow.
questions.e: Brahman and Śakti in one vocabulary, Prakāśa and Vimarśa in another, stillness and movement, ground and flow: the same architecture under many names, which returns in technical dress later in the course.

questions.q: In the practical experiment, Sarah’s worry about her daughter races ahead. What does Swamiji suggest she do?
o: Name it softly as a simulation her mind is running now, and feel her feet on the floor for a breath.
Argue with the worry until she has shown it to be mistaken, and only then feel her feet on the floor.
Make the worry go away at once, and then stop thinking about her daughter for the rest of the day.
Plan carefully for every outcome, so that when the future arrives she will be ready for it in full.
questions.e: She is to see whether it loosens its grip even slightly. James is to add the words “right now, in this situation” to a hardened label, and Kai to treat a replayed failure as tonight’s edit, not the original footage.
questions.c: Name the simulation and come back to now

questions.q: “When James catches a hardened label such as ‘this child is a troublemaker’ and adds the words ‘right now, in this situation,’ the wall turns back into a workable distinction.”
questions.e: Swamiji says to catch the hardened label in himself or a student and add one word of context. James says he does that labelling constantly. The aim is to turn the absolute back into the contextual, not to wipe out distinctions.
questions.c: Turn the absolute back into the contextual
